Algeria.d:
Two outside forces show up in Algeria's record, and both still shape the country. One came from inside: a cocaine network that reached the head of the national police. The other came from next door: Morocco, which journalists reported had marked thousands of Algerian phones for spying.

Start with the police. Abdelghani Hamel was Director-General of National Security, the national police chief, the man in charge of the force that is supposed to stop drug smuggling. In May 2018 customs found 701 kilograms of cocaine at the port of Oran. The seizure exposed the network behind it, and Hamel was removed. Military and civilian courts later convicted him in 2019–2020, along with several generals. The convictions were for corruption and illicit enrichment, not for drugs; Algeria published little about the trafficking case itself, so that is the record that exists.

Then the phones. In 2021 the Pegasus Project, a group of journalists working with Amnesty International, reported that Morocco had selected more than 6,000 Algerian phones as targets for Pegasus, spyware made by the Israeli firm NSO Group that can read everything on a phone. The list included politicians and senior military officers. Morocco denied using Pegasus. Algeria cut diplomatic relations with Morocco in August 2021 and named the alleged spying among its reasons.

On this map Algeria belongs to two patterns: organised crime inside the state, where the Hamel case is proven, and spyware for hire, where Algeria is a place it was used against. The Muslim Brotherhood is also recorded as present.
Algeria.imp: The police chief case shows that a drug network reached the very top of the force meant to police it, and that the courts dealt with it as corruption while the trafficking side stayed largely out of public view. Algerians still do not have a full account of who else was involved. The Pegasus reporting means senior officials' private communications may have been read by a neighbouring government. Watch for whether the Oran trafficking files are ever published, and for any official findings on the spying.

Angola.d:
Angola's record is about money and who handles it. Today its finance minister, the person who decides how the state's money is spent and borrowed, is Vera Daves de Sousa, in office since 8 October 2019. She is listed among the alumni of the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme. The Forum is the organisation behind the Davos meetings; each year it picks people under about 40 for a five-year network of meetings and courses. Being in that network is not wrongdoing. It is recorded here because it is one way private forums keep close ties with the people who run state finances.

Two finished cases show how outside companies and movements have reached into Angola. In January 2025 a Swiss federal court convicted Trafigura, one of the world's largest oil and metals traders, and its former chief operating officer Mike Wainwright over €4.3 million in bribes paid in 2009–11 to an Angolan official linked to a subsidiary of Sonangol, the state oil company. Trafigura was fined $3.3 million and ordered to pay $145.6 million; Wainwright got 32 months, 20 of them suspended. Trafigura has appealed, so the ruling is not final.

The second case went the other way: the state pushing a foreign religious body out. The Brazilian-run Universal Church of the Kingdom of God built a large following in Angola. After Angolan pastors accused its Brazilian leaders of racial discrimination and of pressing pastors into vasectomies, the government in June 2020 ordered the church's board dissolved and removed Bishop Honorilton Gonçalves. The church had already been suspended for 60 days in 2013 after a deadly crush at a Luanda stadium event.

Angola sits in the patterns on global firms buying governments, private forums where officials meet money, and churches placing members in the state. Many other organisations are recorded as present, including Odebrecht, the Gülen movement and the Order of Malta.
Angola.imp: Angola's oil money passes through state companies, and the Trafigura case shows a foreign trader paying an official to get at it; the conviction came from a Swiss court, not an Angolan one. Angolans mostly learn about such deals when other countries prosecute. The finance minister's place in a Davos network is lawful, but it is a channel of influence most citizens never see. Watch the outcome of Trafigura's appeal and whether Angola opens its own cases.

Benin.d: This is an estimate. Nothing is documented on the map for Benin yet: no case of an outside group placing people in its government, police, courts or companies has been recorded. The only organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status. Two French Masonic bodies, the Grand Orient de France and the Grande Loge Nationale Française, are judged likely to be present but are not documented. The conditions scores show a moderate chance of powerful groups inside the state and weak checks to catch them. As a best guess, the most likely route in is the one seen in neighbouring French-speaking states, where senior officials belong to lodges linked to Paris.
Benin.imp: No case means nothing has been found, not that nothing is happening. With moderate risk and weak checks, influence could sit inside the state without anyone recording it. For people in Benin, the thing to watch is who holds the top offices and what networks they belong to, especially lodges tied to France, which have reached presidencies elsewhere in the region.

Botswana.d: This is an estimate. Nothing is documented on the map for Botswana yet, and no organisation from the map's list is recorded as present or even judged likely. The conditions scores are among the better ones in the region: a lower-than-average chance of powerful outside groups sitting inside the state, and checks on power, such as courts and a free press, that are fairly strong. As a best guess, if an outside force did reach in, the most likely route would be the one most common across Africa on this map: a foreign company paying officials for contracts or licences, which usually comes to light only when a court in another country takes up the case.
Botswana.imp: Botswana's empty record fits its fairly strong checks, but an empty record can also mean no one has looked. For people living there, the main thing to watch is how big state contracts and licences are awarded, and whether foreign courts or regulators ever name Botswana officials in bribery cases.

Burkina Faso.d:
Right now a Russian military unit is based just outside Burkina Faso's capital. That is the most important fact in the country's record. Burkina Faso is run by a military government under Captain Ibrahim Traoré, which ordered French troops out in early 2023. On 24 January 2024 personnel from Russia's Africa Corps arrived, an initial 100 to be expanded to 300. Africa Corps is the Russian defence ministry's unit that took over most of the work of the Wagner Group, a private military company Russia used to send fighters and advisers to African governments. It set up its first African base at Loumbila, north-east of Ouagadougou. Ghana's president alleged that a mine had been given to Wagner as payment; Burkina's mines minister denied it.

The older background is about Freemasonry, a fraternal order organised in lodges, which has been close to power in many French-speaking African states. In 2012 the magazine Jeune Afrique reported that President Blaise Compaoré, who ruled from 1987 to 2014, was a former grand master of the Grande Loge du Burkina, and that his foreign minister, Djibrill Bassolé, had succeeded him in that post. These are reports, not findings by any court, and being a Mason is not a crime; the map records them because the head of a lodge and the head of state were the same people.

Burkina Faso sits in two patterns: Russia's networks in Europe and Africa, where it is a target country, and French lodges and African presidencies.
Burkina Faso.imp: A foreign army now works directly with the country's military government, and the terms are not public, including the alleged mine payment, which the government denies. People in Burkina Faso have little way to see what the Russian presence costs or what it is given in return. The lodge reports describe an earlier era when the president and foreign minister led the same private order. Watch for mining concessions granted to Russian-linked firms.

Burundi.d:
Burundi's one documented case concerns a tobacco company and the laws meant to control smoking. British American Tobacco (BAT) is one of the world's largest tobacco firms. In November 2015 BBC Panorama reported on leaked BAT records, from a former employee, that name payments to officials in Burundi. A 2021 analysis by the University of Bath's tobacco research group says payments in Burundi, Comoros, Rwanda and Uganda were aimed at frustrating tobacco control laws modelled on the World Health Organization's treaty on tobacco control.

The status matters here. These are reports based on leaked documents. The UK Serious Fraud Office investigated and closed the case in 2021 without charges, and BAT denies the allegations. The map rates the case as probable, not proven.

Burundi belongs to the pattern on industries inside their regulators, meaning companies that work on the officials who are supposed to regulate them. Also recorded as present are the Order of Malta and the Atlas Network, a US-based network of free-market think tanks. The conditions scores are high: a strong chance of powerful groups sitting inside the state and weak checks to catch them.
Burundi.imp: If the leaked records are right, the officials who were meant to write tobacco rules were being paid by the industry those rules would limit. That affects public health, and ordinary people would never see it. No one has been charged, so the case stays unproven. With weak checks in place, watch how tobacco laws move, or stall, and who argues against them.

Cabo Verde.d: This is an estimate. Nothing is documented on the map for Cabo Verde yet. The only organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status in many countries; its presence is not a case of infiltration. The conditions scores are among the best in Africa on this map: a low chance of powerful groups sitting inside the state, and fairly strong checks such as courts and a free press. As a best guess, the most likely route in would be the one seen in other West African island and coastal states on this map: drug-trafficking networks moving cocaine toward Europe, which in nearby countries have reached police and port officials.
Cabo Verde.imp: Cabo Verde's record is empty and its checks are comparatively strong. For people living there, the risk to watch is the sea route: if cocaine traffickers use the islands, the first signs would be seizures that vanish or port and police officials who are never charged, as has happened elsewhere along the coast.

Cameroon.d:
Cameroon is home to an arrangement that still ties six countries' money to France. The Bank of Central African States (BEAC), based in Yaoundé, issues the CFA franc for Cameroon, the Central African Republic, Chad, the Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea and Gabon. The French Treasury guarantees the currency's fixed exchange rate with the euro, and in return the member states must deposit half their foreign-exchange reserves with it. West Africa's CFA zone dropped that rule from 2021 after a 2019 reform. For Central Africa it is unchanged, and a French Senate report in December 2024 called the reform incomplete. This is open and acknowledged, not secret, but it means a foreign treasury holds half the reserves of the region's central bank.

The older case is stranger. In December 1999 the French newspaper Le Monde reported that President Paul Biya had given tens of millions of francs between 1988 and 1992 to OSTI and CIRCES, Templar-style orders led by Raymond Bernard, including 40 million francs personally. It reported that 11.2 million francs moved from SNH, Cameroon's state oil company, to Bernard's personal account. The presidency called Bernard an "old friend" and would not comment on the payments. Bernard was questioned in the Solar Temple inquiry but was not charged.

Cameroon sits in the patterns on churches and movements placing members in the state and on French lodges and African presidencies. Opus Dei, the Gülen movement, Glencore and Prigozhin's Russian disinformation network are also recorded as present; Wagner and two French lodges are judged likely.
Cameroon.imp: Half of the region's foreign reserves are held by the French Treasury, which gives France a say over money that belongs to Cameroonians and their neighbours. The arrangement is public, but few people know it. The OSTI reporting showed state oil money reaching a private order's leader with no public account. Watch whether the Central African reserve rule is changed, as West Africa's was.

Central African Republic.d:
In the Central African Republic, Russian fighters have guarded the president and fought for the army since 2018, and recent reporting says what is left of their network now runs a drug trade inside the state. About 1,000 fighters from the Wagner Group, a Russian private military company tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, arrived after a Russia–CAR military agreement in August 2018. They protect President Faustin-Archange Touadéra and fought rebels beside the national army, for example at Boyali in January 2021. Reporting links the deployment to gold, diamond and timber concessions. Russia's defence ministry is moving these structures under its Africa Corps; the CAR remains its largest African deployment, estimated at 1,500–2,000.

The link reached the president's own office. Valery Zakharov, a Russian, served as Touadéra's national security adviser from 2018. Ukraine's security service said he headed Wagner's security firm in the country, and the US Treasury sanctioned him as linked to Wagner; the listing shows he also held a Central African passport issued in June 2018.

The newest material, from 2026, is suspected rather than proven. Wall Street Journal reporting from Bangui describes Wagner remnants supplying tramadol, a prescription opioid, to the presidential guard and a youth militia, with senior security officials alleged to control the market. The pills come from Indian manufacturers through Congo and are taken by miners and fighters; university research links rising use to deadlier fighting over mining areas. A research group, GI-TOC, estimates illicit gold exports at $180 million a year, flown out on military cargo planes and laundered through UAE-linked exporters, alongside a state-backed fuel monopoly. A US-sponsored research centre assesses that the old Wagner has in effect taken over the state. Nothing has been charged.

The background includes former president François Bozizé (2003–2013), reported to have joined Freemasonry under the sponsorship of Congo's president. The CAR is central to Russia's networks in Africa and to the patterns on organised crime and criminal money.
Central African Republic.imp: Foreign fighters protect the president, a foreign national advised him on security, and researchers now say the same network sells drugs to his guard. When the forces meant to protect the state are part of the trade, ordinary people have no one to report it to. The gold and fuel money leaves the country rather than funding services. Watch whether the Africa Corps handover changes anything, and whether any of the 2026 allegations reach a court.

Chad.d:
Chad is one of the few countries on this map where a court has convicted senior security officials over drugs. On 24 July 2020 a court in N'Djamena sentenced ten people over a transnational network trafficking tramadol, a prescription painkiller. Among them were high-ranking security and intelligence officials. Analysts at the Institute for Security Studies who read the court documents described a network with strong Chadian connections and large sums moving among its members, some used to try to corrupt judges and the security services. With army and intelligence figures involved, enforcement runs into the very institutions expected to carry it out.

Turkey has also reached into Chad's government. Turkey treats the Gülen movement, a religious network that ran schools around the world, as a terrorist group. In November 2017 the Chadian presidency said President Idriss Déby had agreed to hand the movement's schools to Turkey's state Maarif Foundation by 18 December 2017 and to expel people linked to the movement.

The older background is the president himself. Idriss Déby, who ruled from 1990 to 2021, was named as a Freemason in 2009 reporting on African heads of state and again in a 2013 Jeune Afrique dossier. No lodge is named and nothing more is established.

Chad sits in the patterns on organised crime inside the state (proven), Turkey's pursuit of the Gülen movement, and French lodges and African presidencies. It is also a member of the Central African currency union whose reserves are partly held by the French Treasury.
Chad.imp: The tramadol trial proves that people inside Chad's army and intelligence services were part of a drug network, and that the network tried to buy judges. People in Chad have reason to doubt that the security services can police themselves. The school handover shows a foreign government getting its way over who teaches Chadian children. Watch whether more officials are charged and whether convicted officers return to posts.

Comoros.d:
The biggest case in the Comoros is a former president jailed for life over the sale of passports. Under a 2008 "economic citizenship" law the country sold passports in bulk to stateless people, known as bidoon, living in the Gulf states, with Gulf money paying for them. The scheme was run with Bashar Kiwan, a Syrian-French businessman. Prosecutors said it brought in about 200 million dollars, much of which never reached the treasury. On 28 November 2022 a court in Moroni sentenced former president Ahmed Abdallah Sambi to life in prison for high treason and related charges; Kiwan was tried with him. The passport-sale industry is recorded as present.

The second case is about tobacco. British American Tobacco (BAT) is the world's second-largest listed tobacco company. In November 2015 BBC Panorama, using documents from a former BAT employee, reported that BAT arranged bribes totalling about $26,000 for officials in Rwanda, Burundi and the Comoros, including payments aimed at frustrating tobacco control laws based on the WHO treaty. A 2021 University of Bath study of leaked records counted 236 payments worth $601,502 from 2008 to 2013 across ten African countries. The UK Serious Fraud Office investigated from 2017 and closed the case in January 2021 without charges. BAT denied wrongdoing, so this part is probable, not proven.

The Comoros sits in the pattern on industries inside their regulators. The conditions scores are high, with weak checks on power.
Comoros.imp: Selling a country's citizenship put its passports in the hands of buyers chosen by others, and prosecutors say most of the money never reached the public. A court did convict the former president, which is rare. The tobacco reporting suggests officials writing health rules were paid by the industry, though no charges followed. Watch how citizenship is granted now and how the tobacco laws are enforced.

Congo, Dem. Rep..d:
The most serious case in the Democratic Republic of Congo is happening now in the east, where a neighbouring government is reported to be running a parallel state. M23 is an armed group whose political arm is called the AFC. It took the city of Goma in January 2025 and Bukavu after it. In June 2025 the UN Group of Experts, the panel that reports to the Security Council on Congo, found that M23 operates under Rwandan command, that Rwandan army reinforcements backed the capture of Goma, and that officials said President Kagame decided to take both cities. It described a "systematic effort to dismantle existing State authority": new governors appointed, Rwandans placed over mining, tax, banking and border control, and 18 customary chiefs removed. Rwanda denies directing M23.

The Congolese army has also brought in foreign help. Erik Prince, founder of the US military contractor Blackwater, was the subject of a proposed mercenary deal for North Kivu described in a 2023 UN report, and in February 2026 Reuters reported that he sent men and drones to help the army secure the eastern city of Uvira.

Mining companies are the other route in. Dan Gertler, an Israeli mining and oil investor and a long-time friend of former president Joseph Kabila, was sanctioned by the US Treasury in December 2017 for hundreds of millions of dollars of opaque and corrupt mining and oil deals made through that friendship. Under a later settlement his Ventora group returned licences and agreed to pay royalties to Gécamines, the state miner. He denies wrongdoing. Glencore, a Swiss-based commodity trader, paid $27.5 million to third parties from 2007 to 2018 intending part to bribe Congolese officials, according to US authorities, and in December 2022 agreed to pay Congo $180 million to settle.

Congo sits in the patterns on governments buying officials in other countries and global firms buying governments.
Congo, Dem. Rep..imp: In the east, Congolese people are living under governors, tax collectors and border officials reported to answer to another country, and the mines there are under the same control. Elsewhere the record shows foreign firms getting mining rights through friendship with a president or through bribes, with settlements that bring back only part of the money. Watch who controls mining revenue in North and South Kivu, and what Erik Prince's contract with the army covers.

Congo, Rep..d:
The Republic of Congo, with its capital Brazzaville, has a sitting president who is reported to head the national Masonic lodge. Denis Sassou-Nguesso is reported, in 2009 reporting and a 2013 Jeune Afrique dossier, to be Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Congo-Brazzaville, which is linked to the Grande Loge Nationale Française, one of France's main Masonic bodies. Freemasonry is a fraternal order organised in lodges; membership is lawful. The map records this because the head of state and the head of a private order with ties to Paris are reported to be the same person. Elsewhere on the map, the same reporting says Sassou-Nguesso sponsored the initiation of François Bozizé, later president of the Central African Republic.

The older case is his predecessor. Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that Pascal Lissouba, president from 1992 to 1997, had been initiated at a Grand Orient de France lodge in Besançon. The Grand Orient is France's largest Masonic body.

Both cases are reports, rated possible, not proven by any court. The country belongs to the pattern on French lodges and African presidencies. It is also a member of the Central African currency union whose reserves are partly held by the French Treasury. The commodity trader Gunvor is recorded as present, and the Italian oil company Eni is judged likely.
Congo, Rep..imp: If the reports are right, the president also leads a lodge connected to France, which gives that network a private line to the top of the state that citizens cannot see into. Membership itself is lawful, and nothing here is a court finding. Watch for officials, judges and business partners who share the same lodge, and for how oil deals with foreign traders are made.

Cote d'Ivoire.d:
Côte d'Ivoire's single documented case dates from 2012 and concerns Freemasonry, the fraternal order organised in lodges that has long been close to power in French-speaking Africa. Jeune Afrique reported that year that Prime Minister Jeannot Ahoussou-Kouadio and Interior Minister Hamed Bakayoko were Freemasons. The interior minister runs the police and internal security. The magazine also said the state prosecutor, Simplice Koffi Kouadio, had been received by the Grande Loge de Côte d'Ivoire. It said President Alassane Ouattara was not officially known to be a member. This is a magazine report, rated possible; membership of a lodge is lawful.

Other organisations are recorded as present without a documented case here: Opus Dei, the commodity traders Glencore and Gunvor, and the Russian disinformation network built by Yevgeny Prigozhin, which Facebook found targeting the country in 2019. Elsewhere on the map, Glencore's UK arm pleaded guilty to bribery that included Côte d'Ivoire. The country sits in the pattern on French lodges and African presidencies.
Cote d'Ivoire.imp: The report placed the head of government, the minister over the police and the chief prosecutor in or near the same private lodge, which means people who should check each other may meet as brothers. That is not illegal, but citizens cannot see it. Watch for the same lodge ties among judges and security chiefs, and for commodity deals with foreign traders.

Djibouti.d:
In Djibouti today, China holds much of the country's debt and has a military base there. China opened its first overseas military base in Djibouti in 2017. A China Merchants subsidiary bought 23.5 percent of the Port of Djibouti in 2013. A US Congressional Research Service brief from June 2025 says Chinese institutions hold more than half of Djibouti's 2.6 billion dollars of foreign debt, including a 1.2 billion dollar loan from China's Exim Bank. Djibouti suspended repayments in 2022 and later agreed a moratorium. US officials have warned the debt "could give Beijing undue leverage". Djibouti says it will not hand port control to China. The map rates this as possible: the debt is documented, the leverage is a warning.

The proven case involves a company. Ericsson, the Swedish telecoms equipment maker, agreed in December 2019 to pay more than $1 billion to settle US criminal and civil cases over corruption from 2000 to 2016 in several countries. In Djibouti it admitted paying about €2.1 million to high-ranking officials to win a contract with Djibouti Telecom, the state-owned phone company. In 2022 leaked internal Ericsson files described corruption in at least ten countries.

Djibouti sits in the patterns on China's reach abroad and companies inside other companies.
Djibouti.imp: When one foreign government holds over half a country's debt and has troops on its soil, that government gains weight in decisions about ports and money, even without any secret deal. Djiboutians cannot see the loan terms. The Ericsson case shows officials at the state phone company took bribes, and it was settled in the US, not tried in Djibouti. Watch what happens to the port if repayments stall again.

Egypt.d:
In Egypt today the Muslim Brotherhood is banned as a terrorist organisation, a little over a decade after one of its members was elected president. The Brotherhood is an Islamist movement based in Egypt that seeks to shape the state through politics and preaching. Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure, won the presidential election in June 2012. The army removed him on 3 July 2013, and most of the Brotherhood's leadership was jailed in the following months. On 25 December 2013, two days after a car bomb at the Mansoura police headquarters killed 14 people, the interim cabinet declared the Brotherhood a terrorist organisation; another group, Ansar Bait al-Maqdis, claimed the bombing. Membership became punishable by up to five years in prison, and the designation stays in force. Morsi was later accused of passing state secrets to Qatar; in September 2017 Egypt's highest appeals court upheld his life sentence for leading an illegal group but threw out a 15-year term for stealing documents. Qatar denied the accusations.

The older background shows foreign powers reaching in. After the ruler Khedive Ismail went bankrupt in 1876, Britain and France took joint control of Egypt's finances. Evelyn Baring, of the Barings banking family, became the British controller, although Barings Bank held a large stake in Egyptian debt. He later ran Egypt as British agent and consul-general from 1883 to 1907, keeping its revenues committed to its European creditors. In 1976 Egypt's intelligence chief, Kamal Hassan Ali, signed the charter of the Safari Club, a secret alliance of five intelligence services with France, Saudi Arabia, Morocco and Iran, documented later by the journalist Mohamed Heikal.

Egypt sits in the patterns on movements that sought the state itself, banks and banking families, the Cold War anticommunist web, and exposure and purge.
Egypt.imp: The Brotherhood case shows a movement winning the presidency through an election, then being removed by the army and banned. Being a member is now a crime, and people's links to it can be used against them. The Baring story shows how foreign lenders once ran the country's budget for their own repayment. Watch how the terrorism designation is applied to ordinary people, and who holds Egypt's debts today.

Equatorial Guinea.d:
Right now Russian troops help protect the president of Equatorial Guinea. Teodoro Obiang has ruled the country since 1979. In autumn 2024 Russia deployed up to 200 troops from Africa Corps, the Russian defence ministry's unit that took over most of the Wagner Group's African operations, to guard his presidency and to train elite units in the cities of Malabo and Bata, according to the security journal CTC Sentinel and other analyses. Obiang officially received the Africa Corps commander in Malabo in November 2025. The map rates the deployment as probable.

Other organisations are recorded as present. Glencore, a Swiss-based commodity trader, is one; elsewhere on the map its UK arm pleaded guilty to bribery that included Equatorial Guinea. The country is also a member of the Central African currency union whose reserves are partly held by the French Treasury.

Equatorial Guinea sits in the pattern on Russia's networks in Europe and Africa. Its conditions scores are among the worst on the map: a very high chance of powerful groups sitting inside the state and very weak checks to catch them.
Equatorial Guinea.imp: When a foreign army guards a long-ruling president and trains his elite units, those forces owe something to that foreign government, and people in Equatorial Guinea have no say in the arrangement. With very weak checks, there is little chance of learning its terms. Watch for oil or mining deals with Russian-linked firms, and for how the guarded units are used at home.

Eritrea.d: This is an estimate. Nothing is documented on the map for Eritrea yet. The only organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status in many countries; its presence is not a case. The conditions scores are among the worst on the map: a very high chance of powerful groups sitting inside the state and very weak checks such as courts and a free press. That combination also means little would come to light. As a best guess, the most likely route in would be a foreign government offering security or military help in exchange for influence, the pattern seen in several nearby states on this map.
Eritrea.imp: An empty record in a country with very weak checks says more about what can be seen than about what is happening. People in Eritrea would have few ways to learn of outside influence. The thing to watch is foreign military or security agreements, which elsewhere in the region have brought foreign forces close to the head of state.

Eswatini.d: This is an estimate. Nothing is documented on the map for Eswatini yet, and no organisation from the map's list is recorded as present or judged likely. The conditions scores are on the high side: a fairly strong chance of powerful groups sitting inside the state, and weak checks such as courts and a free press. As a best guess, the most likely route in would be the one most common across southern Africa on this map: a foreign company winning state contracts or licences through payments to officials, usually exposed only when investigators or courts in another country act.
Eswatini.imp: No case is on record, but the weak checks mean influence could go unrecorded. For people in Eswatini, the main thing to watch is how big state contracts are awarded and to whom, and whether officials appear in foreign bribery cases. Leaked company records and court cases abroad are often the first place such payments show up.

Ethiopia.d:
Ethiopia's prime minister today is a Pentecostal Christian who sometimes preaches. Abiy Ahmed converted after the 1998–2000 war with Eritrea. He attends, and sometimes preaches at, the Ethiopian Full Gospel Believers' Church. He became prime minister in 2018 and in 2019 formed the Prosperity Party, which governs today. Personal faith is not wrongdoing; the map records it under the pattern on churches and movements in the state because Pentecostal and evangelical networks are a route by which religious movements gain ties to leaders.

The other case concerns the African Union, the body that brings Africa's governments together, whose headquarters are in Addis Ababa. China built and paid for the roughly $200 million building, which opened in 2012, and the Chinese firm Huawei supplied most of its computer and network equipment. On 26 January 2018 the French newspaper Le Monde, confirmed by the Financial Times, reported that the AU's IT staff had found in 2017 that its computers had been copying data every night to servers in Shanghai, and that microphones were hidden in walls and furniture. The AU replaced its servers and declined Chinese offers to set them up. China's ambassador called the report "ridiculous and preposterous", and Huawei said its equipment was not the source; no public evidence of a backdoor has been shown. The map rates it probable.

Ethiopia sits in the patterns on China's reach abroad, churches and movements in the state, and the infiltration of international bodies.
Ethiopia.imp: If the reporting is right, a foreign government could read the internal data of the body where African governments negotiate with each other, for five years. That affects every member state, not only Ethiopia. The prime minister's faith is his own, but Ethiopians may want to know which church networks have access to him. Watch who builds and runs the computer systems in government buildings.

Gabon.d:
In Gabon the national Masonic lodge has for decades been led by the head of state, and after the 2023 coup that link is being renegotiated. Freemasonry is a fraternal order organised in lodges; membership is lawful. In October 2023 the Grand Lodge of Gabon replaced the deposed president, Ali Bongo, as grand master with Jacques Denis Tsanga, governor of Haut-Ogooué province and a former minister of water and forests. The post had traditionally gone to the president, and the transitional leader, Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema, reportedly declined it. In November 2023, according to Africa Intelligence as reported by Gabonreview, the grand master of the Grand Orient de France, France's largest Masonic body, met Oligui in Libreville in secret and offered support to his transitional council, describing Oligui as a non-practising Freemason. Oligui was elected president in April 2025.

The roots go back to Omar Bongo, initiated in 1953 and president from 1967 until his death in 2009. He founded two Masonic bodies, one tied to the Grand Orient de France and one to the Grande Loge Nationale Française, and was grand master until he died. In 2009 the French lodge's grand master installed his son Ali as grand master, the same year Ali became president; ministers and the head of the National Security Council attended. In 2012 Jeune Afrique reported that the police chief, Antoine Embinga, a lodge grand master, had been removed.

Gabon is the clearest case in the pattern on French lodges and African presidencies, and also appears under lodges inside police and courts. These are press reports, rated probable or possible.
Gabon.imp: For over fifty years, Gabon's president and the head of its main lodges were often the same man, with ministers and the police chief inside the same order, and French lodges involved in choosing its leaders. Citizens could not see what was settled there. The new president has reportedly kept his distance from the grand mastership, but French lodge leaders still seek him out. Watch who the new grand masters are and what posts they hold.

Gambia.d:
The Gambia's cases come from the rule of Yahya Jammeh, who left office in 2017, and the networks he let into the state. Their effects are still felt.

One case is about timber. Between 2014 and 2017 The Gambia exported nearly $163 million of rosewood to China, although its own rosewood was almost gone by 2011. Most came from Senegal's Casamance region, where logging funds armed groups. Westwood Company, which held the exclusive export licence, was co-founded by Swiss national Nicolae Bogdan Buzaianu and President Jammeh himself, according to the Swiss group TRIAL International, which filed a criminal complaint for pillage with Switzerland's Attorney General in June 2019. The Environmental Investigation Agency documented the trade in 2020. This is an allegation, not a court finding.

The other case involves Hezbollah, the Lebanese Shia party and armed group; the US designates several West African traders as its financiers. In March 2019 the reporting network OCCRP showed that Mohamed Bazzi, designated by the US as a key Hezbollah financier, was one of Jammeh's closest associates and was given monopolies including the fuel supply. Ali Charara, also designated, paid 35 million dollars for half of the state telecoms firms Gamtel and Gamcel, and OCCRP estimated that over 100 million dollars from Gambian telecoms reached Hezbollah.

The Gambia sits in the patterns on organised crime inside the state and Iran's armed allies inside governments.
Gambia.imp: Under Jammeh, the fuel supply, phone companies and timber exports were handed to his associates and, by the reporting, to financiers of a foreign armed group. That money left the country rather than paying for services, and the timber trade funded conflict next door. Gambians are still owed a full account. Watch the Swiss complaint and who controls Gamtel, Gamcel and the fuel trade now.

Ghana.d:
In Ghana, Freemasonry is openly part of political life today. Freemasonry is a fraternal order organised in lodges; membership is lawful. At his parliamentary vetting on 22 January 2025, George Opare Addo, nominated as Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment, was asked by the minority leader, Alexander Afenyo-Markin, whether he was a Freemason. He said yes and named his lodge, "Amity". He was confirmed in President Mahama's government. Afenyo-Markin had himself said in February 2024: "I am a Freemason and a Catholic." In May 2024 the Grand Lodge of Ghana honoured the Asantehene, the Ashanti king Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, for 25 years in Freemasonry; GhanaWeb reported that the National Security and Transport ministers took part as members. Former President John Kufuor has said he joined in 1967. The map records these because they show how many office-holders share one network, not because any wrongdoing is alleged.

The older case is about drugs. In 2006, seventy-seven parcels of cocaine landed from a ship, the MV Benjamin, and disappeared. A recording then surfaced of a senior police officer meeting suspects at his home. A committee of enquiry led by a Supreme Court judge found the police account unsatisfactory, and the officer returned to duty.

Ghana sits in the pattern on organised crime inside the state. Airbus and the Tony Blair Institute are also recorded as present.
Ghana.imp: Ghana is unusual in that lodge membership is asked about and answered in public, so citizens can see which ministers belong. That openness is what other countries on this map lack. The cocaine case shows the opposite: a senior officer was caught on tape meeting suspects and went back to work. Watch whether drug cases involving police reach court, and whether vetting questions about membership continue.

Guinea.d:
Guinea's most serious case was decided by a foreign court and concerns one of the world's largest untapped iron ore deposits, at Simandou. In 2008 Guinea's government took blocks I and II from the mining company Rio Tinto and gave them to BSG Resources, controlled by the Israeli businessman Beny Steinmetz. On 22 January 2021 a court in Geneva found Steinmetz guilty of corruption over bribes paid to Mamadie Touré, a wife of President Lansana Conté, to obtain the rights. He was sentenced to five years and a fine of 50 million Swiss francs, and Swiss appeal courts upheld the conviction in 2022 and 2023. Steinmetz denies wrongdoing.

Drugs reached the president's family in the same era. After Conté died, the junta that took power arrested his son Ousmane Conté in February 2009 and charged him with trafficking. He confessed on state television to involvement in the cocaine trade; it was not clear whether the confession was coerced. The US Treasury designated him a drug kingpin in 2010 while he was in prison in Conakry. No court verdict followed.

Turkey also reached in. Turkey treats the Gülen movement, a religious network that ran schools abroad, as a terrorist group, and by June 2017 the movement's schools in Guinea had been taken over by Turkey's state Maarif Foundation after talks through Turkey's Foreign Ministry. And in 2012 Jeune Afrique reported that President Alpha Condé oversaw the Grande Loge de Guinée, a Masonic lodge; that is a report, rated possible.

Guinea sits in the patterns on organised crime inside the state, Turkey's pursuit of the Gülen movement, and French lodges and African presidencies.
Guinea.imp: The Simandou case shows how a mining right worth a fortune was obtained by paying a president's wife, and it was a Swiss court, not a Guinean one, that said so. The president's son confessed to cocaine dealing on television, but no court ever ruled. People in Guinea have seen admissions without judgments. Watch who now holds the Simandou rights and on what terms.

Guinea-Bissau.d:
Guinea-Bissau has served since the mid-2000s as a stopping point for South American cocaine headed to Europe, and the trade has reached its entire military command. The most recent case is happening now. The director of the judicial police said in February 2022 that 975 of 980 kilograms of cocaine seized in November 2021 had disappeared from official custody, and that police and security personnel were suspected of taking it. One officer was arrested. The country had not tried a drug case since 2005.

The roots are in the US cases of 2013. On 2 April 2013 the US Drug Enforcement Administration arrested the former navy chief, José Américo Bubo Na Tchuto, at sea in a sting; he pleaded guilty in New York to conspiring to import cocaine. The air force chief, Ibraima Papa Camara, was indicted alongside him and was never handed over. On 18 April 2013 an indictment charged the armed forces chief, General Antonio Indjai, who had led the 2012 coup, with offering to store cocaine for the FARC, the Colombian guerrilla group, and to supply it with weapons including surface-to-air missiles. He stayed in Bissau and was not arrested. With the navy, air force and army chiefs charged in the same period, the whole senior command stood accused at once. In February 2022 President Umaro Sissoco Embaló blamed Na Tchuto, by then back home, for a failed attack on the government palace.

Earlier still, in March 2009, the president, João Bernardo Vieira, and the army chief of staff were killed within hours of each other, when the UN drugs office described the country as at risk of becoming Africa's first narco-state. The link to cocaine is the UN's assessment, not a court finding, and no one was prosecuted.

Guinea-Bissau is one of the central cases in the pattern on organised crime inside the state.
Guinea-Bissau.imp: In Guinea-Bissau, the people charged with stopping drug trafficking were the ones accused of running it, and only a foreign court has convicted any of them. Seized cocaine can vanish from police custody. Ordinary people have no local court that has tried a drug case in two decades. Watch whether the missing 975 kilograms case goes anywhere, and what posts the indicted generals hold.

Kenya.d:
Kenya has more documented cases than any other country in this part of the map, and several are unfolding now. Group them by who reached in.

Foreign governments. Turkey treats the Gülen movement, a religious network, as a terrorist group and seeks its members abroad. On 18 October 2024 four Turkish nationals living in Kenya as refugees were sent back to Turkey after seven people were abducted in Nairobi; a senior Kenyan foreign affairs official confirmed it was "at the request of the government of Türkiye". The UN said it was "deeply concerned". In 2021 Turkish intelligence seized a nephew of Fethullah Gülen in Kenya. Earlier, in 2013, a Kenyan court convicted two Iranians alleged to be members of the Quds Force, the foreign arm of Iran's Revolutionary Guards, of plotting attacks with explosives.

Companies and election firms. In November 2024, a day after directors of the Indian conglomerate Adani were charged with bribery in New York, President William Ruto cancelled Adani's proposed lease of Nairobi's main airport and a power-line deal. Cambridge Analytica, a British political-data firm, ran Uhuru Kenyatta's 2013 and 2017 campaigns, according to its own executive on undercover film, and wrote the party's manifesto. In 2022 the Israeli hacking outfit Team Jorge accessed the Telegram account of Dennis Itumbi, digital strategist for Ruto's campaign.

Organised crime. Two brothers running a Mombasa heroin organisation, the Akashas, admitted in New York in 2018 that they had paid Kenyan judges, prosecutors and police to block their extradition; none of those officials has been named or charged. Harun Mwau, an MP and assistant transport minister over the ports, was designated a drug kingpin by the US in 2011; he denies it. The ICC charged Kenyatta in 2011 with organising attacks by Mungiki, a banned sect, after the 2007–08 election violence that killed about 1,300 people; he denied it, and the charges were withdrawn in 2014 citing witness interference.

Faith networks. Patrick Njoroge, a celibate member of the Catholic organisation Opus Dei, governed the central bank from 2015 to 2023. In 2025 Ruto, an evangelical, announced an 8,000-seat church at State House.
Kenya.imp: Kenyans have seen refugees handed to a foreign government, election campaigns run and hacked by foreign firms, and judges and police paid by heroin traffickers who were never named. Most of this came to light through foreign courts and journalists. The faith ties of leaders are lawful, but critics say a church at State House breaches the secular state. Watch who is named from the Akasha payments and who designs the next campaigns.

Lesotho.d: This is an estimate. Nothing is documented on the map for Lesotho yet. The only organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status in many countries; its presence is not a case. The conditions scores are on the high side: a fairly strong chance of powerful groups sitting inside the state, and weak checks such as courts and a free press. As a best guess, the most likely route in is a foreign company seeking state contracts or licences through payments to officials, the pattern seen most often in southern Africa on this map.
Lesotho.imp: No case is on record, but weak checks mean influence could pass unnoticed. For people in Lesotho, the thing to watch is how large state contracts are awarded and whether officials turn up in foreign bribery investigations. Payments of this kind usually come to light first through courts, regulators or journalists in other countries, so those reports are worth following.

Liberia.d:
In 2026 Liberia's police chief said what many suspected: senior government officials are involved in cocaine trafficking. After the country's largest recorded seizure, close to four tonnes of cocaine bound for Europe, the police inspector general made that statement. The national police charged the head of its own Major Crimes Unit and another official, and named a deputy commander in charge of security at Roberts International Airport as an active participant. Twelve suspects were charged in the seizure case, and a former vice-president was separately indicted on trafficking counts. These are charges, not convictions.

It went differently in 2010. In Operation Relentless, South American and West African traffickers were recorded paying senior Liberian officials to guarantee safe passage and storage for multi-tonne cocaine shipments. The officials reported the approaches and worked with the US Drug Enforcement Administration instead, leading to extraditions and convictions in New York. The DEA called the cooperation from the top of Liberia's government unprecedented.

The older background is Freemasonry, a fraternal order organised in lodges. William Tolbert, president from 1971 to 1980, was Grand Master of the Masonic Order of Liberia. Lodge membership was widely seen as a requirement for leadership in the ruling True Whig Party, and by the 1970s most high officials were Masons. Tolbert was killed in Samuel Doe's coup on 12 April 1980, along with much of the Masonic leadership. Doe banned Freemasonry, later lifted the ban; the order was reinstated in 1988, and Doe himself was initiated in 1989.

Liberia sits in the patterns on organised crime inside the state and French lodges and African presidencies.
Liberia.imp: Liberia shows both outcomes: officials who turned traffickers in, and, today, officials charged with helping them. The current charges reach the police unit and airport security meant to stop the trade. For decades a single lodge was the gateway to office, and its fall came with a coup. Watch how the 2026 cases end and whether higher officials are named.

Libya.d:
Libya has two rival governments, one in Tripoli and one in the east, and outside forces are inside both. Today, fuel is the biggest money stream. Libyan authorities buy fuel at world prices and sell it at home at a heavy subsidy, about 0.15 dinars a litre against two or three dinars on the black market, and it is resold abroad. The International Crisis Group's 2026 assessment is that the racket helps keep the peace between rival elites in Tripoli and Benghazi, who both take a share. UN rules let other states stop suspect cargoes if the Libyan government flags them; no such signal has come in years, which the analysis blames on the complicity of government agencies.

Foreign forces. Khalifa Haftar's Libyan National Army controls the east. A May 2020 UN report counted 800–1,200 fighters from Wagner, a Russian private military company, supporting it. A Pentagon report said the UAE was Wagner's main funder there. Africa Corps, the Russian defence ministry's own unit, began replacing Wagner in spring 2024 and uses eastern bases as logistics hubs. A UN panel found in 2021 that Erik Prince, founder of the US firm Blackwater, broke the arms embargo in a 2019 plan to supply aircraft and personnel to Haftar; he denies it.

Smuggling inside the state. The UN Security Council sanctioned Abd al-Rahman Milad, known as Bija, a serving coast guard commander at Zawiya, in 2018 for fuel smuggling, migrant trafficking and violence at sea. He was detained in 2020 and released without conviction. The US designated a Libyan operator, a Malta company and its vessel in 2020 for smuggling fuel and drugs.

Politics. Khalid al-Mishri, of the party founded as the Libyan Muslim Brotherhood's political arm, chaired the High Council of State in Tripoli from 2018 to 2023.
Libya.imp: Libyans pay for fuel subsidies that are resold abroad, and the profits keep rival elites content rather than funding services. The officials who could stop it are the ones who benefit. Foreign fighters, funded by foreign governments, back one side, and a coast guard commander sanctioned for smuggling went free. Watch who controls fuel exports and how Russia uses its eastern bases.

Madagascar.d:
Madagascar's documented case is about a foreign power trying to shape a presidential election. The Russian investigative outlet Proekt and the BBC reported in 2019 that 15–20 Russian political strategists tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, the businessman behind the Wagner Group, worked on Madagascar's 2018 presidential race and dealt with as many as eight candidates, including the winner, Andry Rajoelina. Candidate André Mailhol said they gave him €5,000 in cash; former prime minister Omer Beriziky said he was promised $2 million. Rajoelina denied being Russia's candidate, and the BBC found no evidence he took Russian money. Prigozhin's representatives denied any link. In October 2019 Facebook removed networks of fake accounts tied to Prigozhin that targeted Madagascar's election among others.

The map rates this probable. Wagner itself is recorded as present. Two French Masonic bodies are judged likely to be present but are not documented.

Madagascar sits in the patterns on Russia's networks in Europe and Africa and on elections for hire.
Madagascar.imp: If the reporting is right, foreign strategists were paying several candidates at once, so whoever won, they had a relationship with the winner. Voters could not see who was funding whom. The winner denies taking Russian money and no evidence shows he did. Watch who advises future campaigns and whether candidates say where their money comes from.

Malawi.d:
Malawi's case is about one businessman and the contracts for its police and army. Zuneth Sattar is a UK-based businessman. In June 2022 Malawi's Anti-Corruption Bureau reported that the police and the Malawi Defence Force had given 16 contracts worth over 150 million dollars between 2017 and 2021 to five companies linked to him. President Lazarus Chakwera said 84 people were named in the report. He withdrew all delegated powers from Vice President Saulos Chilima, and the former police chief George Kainja and the lands minister Kezzie Msukwa were arrested. Chilima denied wrongdoing; he died in a plane crash in June 2024.

The map rates this case probable: it rests on an investigation, not a verdict. British American Tobacco is judged likely to be present, but nothing is documented. Malawi's conditions scores are moderate, better than most of its neighbours.
Malawi.imp: Contracts to supply the police and army are among the hardest for the public to check, and this report says one businessman's companies won over $150 million of them, with a vice-president and a police chief named. Ordinary Malawians pay for those contracts. Watch whether the arrests lead to trials and whether the contracts are recovered.

Mali.d:
Mali's military government now relies on Russian troops. On 6 June 2025 the Wagner Group, the Russian private military company, announced it was leaving Mali. Africa Corps, the Russian defence ministry's unit that took over most of Wagner's African work after Yevgeny Prigozhin's death in 2023, had deployed about 1,000 troops in December 2024 and became the only Russian force there, with about 2,000 Russian troops remaining. Several Wagner commanders moved across. Human Rights Watch and Le Monde have reported killings of civilians by Malian soldiers and Africa Corps members in 2025–26.

How Wagner got in is documented. On 24 July 2023 the US Treasury sanctioned the defence minister, Colonel Sadio Camara, saying he planned and organised Wagner's deployment and travelled to Russia several times in 2021 to finalise it. It also sanctioned the air force chief, Colonel Alou Boi Diarra, for promoting Wagner inside the armed forces, and his deputy, Lieutenant Colonel Adama Bagayoko.

Drug money is moving into the economy. A UN drugs office report from April 2024 found cocaine seizures across Burkina Faso, Chad, Mali, Mauritania and Niger rose from about 13 kilograms a year in 2015–2020 to 1,466 kilograms in 2022, with proceeds flowing into gold and real estate, and named armed groups in Mali among the beneficiaries. No prosecution has followed. The roots go back to 2009, when a Boeing 727 from Venezuela was unloaded at the Tarkint desert airstrip and burned, with UN inquiries pointing to protection by local officials; no senior conviction followed.

In 2012 Jeune Afrique reported that President Amadou Toumani Touré, overthrown that March, oversaw the Grande Loge du Mali. Mali sits in the patterns on Russia's networks, organised crime and criminal money.
Mali.imp: A foreign army now fights alongside Mali's soldiers, and both are reported to have killed civilians. The ministers who brought that army in are known, but the terms are not public. Cocaine money is going into gold and property, and no one has been prosecuted. Watch for who receives gold and mining rights, and whether killings of civilians are investigated.

Mauritania.d: This is an estimate. Nothing is documented on the map for Mauritania yet. Several organisations are recorded as present: the Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status; the Gülen movement, a religious network Turkey pursues abroad; the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist movement; and a group called Fight Impunity. The conditions scores lean high: a fairly strong chance of powerful groups sitting inside the state and weak checks. As a best guess, the most likely route in is drug money: a UN report found Mauritania alone seized 2.3 tonnes of cocaine by mid-2023, with Sahel proceeds flowing into gold and real estate, the route recorded in neighbouring Mali.
Mauritania.imp: No case is recorded, but large cocaine seizures and weak checks make it likely that drug money is reaching officials or businesses somewhere. For people in Mauritania, watch whether seized drugs reach court and who is buying gold and property with unexplained money. Seizures that disappear from custody, as has happened elsewhere in West Africa, would be an early warning sign.

Mauritius.d:
Mauritius's documented case concerns a power station contract. Burmeister & Wain Scandinavian Contractor is a Danish company that builds power plants. In June 2020 the African Development Bank, which lends for projects across the continent, debarred it from its contracts for 21 months. The bank found, "on the balance of probabilities", that the company paid members of the Mauritian administration through intermediaries during tenders for the Saint-Louis power station run by the Central Electricity Board. That is a finding by a lender's sanctions process, not a criminal conviction.

The Grand Orient de France, France's largest Masonic body, is recorded as present; the Grande Loge Nationale Française, the Hindu nationalist RSS and Airbus are judged likely. Mauritius has among the better conditions scores in Africa on this map, with fairly strong checks on power.

The case sits in the pattern on exposure, purge and reversal.
Mauritius.imp: A foreign company was found to have paid Mauritian officials to win a contract for electricity that everyone pays for. It was the lender, not a Mauritian court, that acted, and the officials are not named. Watch whether Mauritius pursues the officials involved, and how future power and infrastructure tenders are run.

Morocco.d:
In June 2026 a court in Casablanca sentenced 29 people in a drug case that reached Morocco's parliament. The case is known as the "Escobar of the Sahara" trial. It began with testimony from a jailed Malian trafficker who said his Moroccan political associates had seized his assets after his arrest in 2019. It covered tonnes of cannabis resin moved across North Africa alongside Latin American cocaine. A construction figure and former head of a regional council got 12 years, and two former MPs from the governing party got 10 years each. Charges included drug and gold trafficking, corruption and laundering. One defendant was acquitted and appeals are open.

Religion and the state are closely bound. Ahmed Toufiq, a historian, has been the king's Minister of Islamic Affairs, who oversees the country's mosques, since November 2002, under five prime ministers. He has said a meeting with the sheikh of the Boutchichiya, Morocco's largest Sufi order, set him on the Sufi path. In August 2025 a leaked letter from Toufiq warned the order about "abuses" and "appetites" during a dispute over its leadership. From 2011 to 2021 the government was led by the PJD, an Islamist party historically linked to the Muslim Brotherhood but never an official branch; it lost 113 seats in 2021. In 2017 Morocco shut schools linked to the Gülen movement, which Turkey pursues abroad.

Morocco also reaches outward. Elsewhere on this map, the 2021 Pegasus Project reported that Morocco selected more than 6,000 Algerian phones for spying with NSO Group's Pegasus software; Morocco denies using it. In 1976 its intelligence chief, Ahmed Dlimi, signed the charter of the Safari Club, a secret alliance of five intelligence services.

Morocco sits in the patterns on organised crime inside the state, movements that sought the state, and the Cold War anticommunist web.
Morocco.imp: The 2026 verdicts show that drug money had reached elected members of the governing party and a regional council, and a court said so. The minister over mosques has held his post for over twenty years and has ties to one Sufi order, which shapes what is preached. Watch the appeals and whether other politicians named in testimony are charged.

Mozambique.d:
Mozambique is still paying for the "tuna bonds", the largest hidden-debt scandal on this part of the map. In 2013–14 three state companies borrowed $622 million from the Swiss bank Credit Suisse and $535 million from Russia's VTB bank, backed by state guarantees that were never shown to parliament or the IMF. The money was for tuna fishing and maritime security projects with the shipbuilder Privinvest. Credit Suisse bankers took kickbacks, about $45 million to one banker, Andrew Pearse, and the US Justice Department said at least $200 million went in bribes and kickbacks to bankers and officials. When $2.2 billion of hidden loans came to light in 2016, the IMF and World Bank froze support; one study estimated two million people were pushed into poverty. Mozambique's Constitutional Council declared the loans void. Credit Suisse pleaded guilty to fraud in the US in 2021. A Brooklyn jury convicted former finance minister Manuel Chang in August 2024; prosecutors said Privinvest paid him $7 million, and he was sentenced to eight and a half years. A London court let Mozambique recover over $825 million from the estate of Privinvest's owner.

Drugs are the other thread, and remain suspected. Researchers documented a heroin trafficking system running for three decades with what they called a tight integration between ruling party figures and traffickers, with near-zero heroin seizures as the evidence. In 2010 the US named a prominent Maputo businessman a drug kingpin and sanctioned his conglomerate, a store and a shopping centre; banks left the centre within a month, but he was never prosecuted.

In 2019 Facebook removed fake-account networks tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, the Russian businessman behind Wagner, that meddled in Mozambique's election.

Mozambique sits in the patterns on global firms buying governments, banks and banking families, criminal money and organised crime.
Mozambique.imp: Bankers and officials hid $2 billion of debt from parliament, took bribes, and left ordinary Mozambicans to bear the cost through frozen aid and lost income. Courts abroad have convicted some of them and returned part of the money. The heroin trade is said to be protected at the top, and no one has been charged at home. Watch the debt recovery and whether drug cases ever reach Mozambican courts.

Namibia.d:
Namibia is in the middle of its biggest corruption trial, the "Fishrot" case, and two former ministers are among the accused. Samherji is one of Iceland's largest fishing companies. On 12 November 2019 WikiLeaks published files, investigated with Icelandic and Al Jazeera journalists and the company's former Namibia manager Jóhannes Stefánsson, showing Samherji paying people close to Namibia's government to obtain quota to catch horse mackerel. A quota is the permission to fish a set amount, and it is worth a lot of money. Fisheries Minister Bernhardt Esau and Justice Minister Sacky Shanghala resigned the next day. In December 2019 they and four associates, known as the "Fishrot Six", were arrested. They are charged with racketeering, corruption and money laundering under Namibia's organised crime law. Iceland also opened an investigation into Samherji.

Samherji denies paying bribes and blames Stefánsson. The case is still before the courts, so the charges are not proven.

The Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret society from South Africa's apartheid era, is judged likely to be present but nothing is documented. Namibia's conditions scores are moderate.
Namibia.imp: Fish in Namibian waters belong to the public, and the charges say a foreign company paid the ministers in charge of them to get a share. The money that should have reached the state went elsewhere. The trial is still running, so nothing is yet proven. Watch the verdict and how fishing quotas are handed out now.

Niger.d:
Niger's military government now works with Russian forces. After the July 2023 coup the junta ended military cooperation with the United States and France. Dozens of troops from Africa Corps, the Russian defence ministry's unit that took over most of the Wagner Group's African work, arrived in the capital, Niamey, in April 2024 and were stationed at Air Base 101 before US forces had left it. Estimates for 2025 put them at 200–300, mostly in intelligence, training and surveillance. Wikipedia's account says they took part in fighting during a January 2026 attack on Niamey airport.

Drugs pass through. Niger sits on the Sahel route that the UN drugs office describes as a natural stopover between South America and Europe. In 2021 a local mayor was arrested with more than 200 kilograms of cocaine in his vehicle; no outcome is documented.

Turkey has also reached in. Turkey treats the Gülen movement, a religious network that ran schools abroad, as a terrorist group, and by June 2017 the movement's schools in Niger were taken over by Turkey's state Maarif Foundation after talks with Turkey's Foreign Ministry.

The background includes Mamadou Tandja, president from 1999 to 2010, named as a Freemason in 2009 reporting; no lodge is named.

Niger sits in the patterns on Russia's networks in Europe and Africa, organised crime, Turkey's pursuit of the Gülen movement, and French lodges and African presidencies.
Niger.imp: A foreign force now works in Niger's intelligence and surveillance, which means it may know more about Nigeriens than they know about it. The terms are not public. A mayor caught with cocaine shows drug money reaching local office, with no known outcome. Watch whether drug cases reach court and what Russia receives in exchange.

Nigeria.d:
Nigeria has many kinds of outside influence on record, and some cases are still in court. Here they are grouped by who reached in.

Organised crime and police. Abba Kyari, a deputy commissioner who led the police Intelligence Response Team, was charged by the national drug agency with swapping seized cocaine and offering an officer money to stop it being tested. He has been detained since 2022. In March 2026 a judge acquitted him on a separate asset-declaration case, calling it persecution; the cocaine trial continues. A BBC investigation in 2021 used leaked documents suggesting money went to the Neo Black Movement, which the BBC linked to the Black Axe confraternity, to "protect votes" in the 2012 Edo governorship election, with 80 government roles as reward. The group denies any link.

Companies. Glencore, a Swiss-based commodity trader, pleaded guilty in 2022 to bribery in Nigeria and other African states. A London court in 2023 voided an $11 billion award won by P&ID, a gas company, after finding it had bribed a Nigerian government lawyer. A Milan court in 2021 acquitted Eni and Shell of corruption over the $1.1 billion OPL 245 oil block, whose money went on to a company controlled by a former oil minister. A 2009 US cable records a Shell executive saying Shell had "seconded people to all the relevant ministries"; Shell rejected that.

Election firms. Cambridge Analytica and Israel's Team Jorge worked in 2015 to re-elect Goodluck Jonathan by discrediting Muhammadu Buhari, who won.

Faith and finance. Yemi Osinbajo, a pastor of the Redeemed Christian Church of God, was vice-president from 2015 to 2023. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala moved from World Bank managing director to finance minister in 2011.

Nigeria's 1999 constitution bars members of secret societies from elected office, a rule commentators apply to the Ogboni fraternities, Freemasons and others. In 1999 a defeated candidate alleged that Olusegun Obasanjo was an Ogboni member; the tribunal dismissed the claim.
Nigeria.imp: Nigerians face influence from several directions at once: a police commander charged with recycling cocaine, a confraternity reported to trade violence for jobs, and foreign oil and commodity firms found to have paid officials. Foreign courts handled most company cases, with mixed results. The constitution bans secret-society members from office, but enforcement depends on proof that is rarely produced. Watch the Kyari trial and the next election's campaign contractors.

Rwanda.d:
Rwanda's documented case is about advisers working inside the centre of government. The Tony Blair Institute for Global Change is a London-based non-profit founded by the former British prime minister that places advisers inside governments; it reports work with more than 45 governments and had about 1,000 staff in 2026. In Rwanda it has supported a Strategy and Policy Unit and a Government Action Coordination Unit and worked on the Imihigo system, in which officials sign performance contracts. Its largest donor is the foundation of Larry Ellison, the US tech billionaire, which gave over £52 million in 2023, according to The Guardian. This work is open and lawful; the map records it because outside advisers sit close to where decisions are made, funded by a private donor.

Rwanda also appears elsewhere on this map as an outside force: a UN expert panel found in 2025 that the M23 armed group in eastern Congo operates under Rwandan command, which Rwanda denies. That case is recorded under Congo. British American Tobacco and NSO Group are recorded as present; leaked BAT records reported by the BBC in 2015 named payments to Rwandan officials. Rwanda sits in the pattern on consultants and lobbyists inside the ministries.
Rwanda.imp: When foreign-funded advisers help run the units that set government priorities, Rwandans may not know whose ideas they are living under or who pays for them. The arrangement is public but not well known. Watch which policies these units shape, and how Rwanda's role in eastern Congo develops. Rwandans can ask who funds the advisers and what they are working on.

Sao Tome and Principe.d: This is an estimate. Nothing is documented on the map for São Tomé and Príncipe yet. The only organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status in many countries; its presence is not a case. The conditions scores are among the better ones on the map, with a low chance of powerful groups sitting inside the state and middling checks on power. As a best guess, the most likely route in is a foreign company or lender seeking state contracts, licences or debt deals, the pattern seen most often among small states on this map.
Sao Tome and Principe.imp: No case is recorded, and the conditions are comparatively good. For people in São Tomé and Príncipe, the thing to watch is large foreign contracts and loans, and who negotiates them. Loans and contracts negotiated in private can tie a small state to one lender or company for years, and the terms are rarely published, so asking to see them is the first step.

Senegal.d:
In Senegal the Mouride brotherhood has a close relationship with the presidency, and the current president continues it. The Mourides are a Sufi Muslim brotherhood with millions of followers, centred on the holy city of Touba, which has run with wide independence from the state since 1928. Presidents court its leader, the caliph. President Bassirou Diomaye Faye, sworn in on 2 April 2024, visited Caliph Serigne Mountakha Mbacké on 15 April 2024, again in August 2024 and March 2025, and on 7 August 2025 before the Grand Magal pilgrimage, and pledged state help with Touba's water and sanitation. Abdoulaye Wade went to Touba the day after his 2000 election and put Mourides in his government. None of this is illegal; the map records it as a religious movement with steady access to the head of state.

Other religious bodies have reached the presidency too. In February 2020, while in office, President Macky Sall was named a laureate of the Sunhak Peace Prize, funded by the Unification Church and carrying a US$1 million award. In 2017 Senegal closed more than a dozen schools linked to the Gülen movement, attended by about 3,000 children, after Turkish requests, and Turkey's state Maarif Foundation opened schools in their place.

The older cases are thinner. In 2012 Jeune Afrique reported that Abdoulaye Wade had been initiated into Freemasonry; Sall denied membership. In 2019 a governing-coalition MP was arrested in a police operation involving cocaine, then released; the case did not reach a verdict.

Senegal sits in the patterns on churches and movements in the state, Turkey's pursuit of the Gülen movement and organised crime.
Senegal.imp: The Mouride caliph has a direct line to every president and Touba gets state help after presidential visits. That is open, but it gives one religious leader weight that other citizens lack. A sitting president accepted $1 million from a church-funded prize. Watch which state projects follow presidential visits, and whether drug cases involving politicians reach court.

Seychelles.d:
The Seychelles' documented case involves a cryptocurrency exchange registered there. KuCoin, run through a company called PEKEN Global Limited, was given a $297 million penalty in 2025 for failing to put effective anti-money-laundering measures in place and failing to report suspicious transactions. Its executives were separately indicted in the United States over US banking-secrecy rules and running an unlicensed money-transmitting business. The exchange was registered in the Seychelles while serving customers in places where it held no licence.

This is a case of criminal money passing through a company, not of officials being bought. It places the Seychelles in the pattern on criminal money inside banks and firms, as a registration base. The Order of Malta is also recorded as present. The country's conditions scores are comparatively good.
Seychelles.imp: Companies can register in the Seychelles and serve customers worldwide without proper checks, which makes the country a convenient base for moving money that should be flagged. The penalty came from the US, not from the Seychelles. Watch whether the Seychelles tightens rules on the companies it registers. Better checks would protect the country's own financial system as well.

Sierra Leone.d:
A Dutch cocaine boss wanted across Europe is reported to be living under high-level protection in Sierra Leone. Jos Leijdekkers, known as "Bolle Jos", was sentenced in his absence in Rotterdam in June 2024 to 24 years for smuggling over 7 tonnes of cocaine, and is on Dutch and EU most-wanted lists. In January 2025 Reuters reported, using video and facial-recognition matches, that he attended a New Year mass two rows behind President Julius Maada Bio in Bio's home town, and three sources said he is married to Bio's daughter Agnes. Dutch prosecutors said he had lived in Sierra Leone for at least six months. The government said it was investigating, that the president did not know him, and denied knowing his whereabouts. The head of immigration was dismissed after footage showed him with Leijdekkers. The map rates this possible.

The background is the Lungi cocaine flight. In July 2008 a twin-engine aircraft carrying around 700 kilograms of cocaine landed at Lungi airport marked with Red Cross symbols. The prosecutions that followed in 2009 reached airport and security staff as well as the foreign crew, and US congressional testimony called them historic for the region. The minister of transport and aviation was dismissed after court proceedings indicated he had given landing clearance for the aircraft, but that allegation was never tried.

Sierra Leone sits in the pattern on organised crime inside the state.
Sierra Leone.imp: If the reporting is right, a convicted cocaine trafficker has married into the president's family and is protected by officials, which would put him beyond the reach of the police. The government denies knowing him. In 2008 the courts did convict airport and security staff, but a minister was only dismissed. Watch whether Leijdekkers is handed over and whether the immigration case leads further.

Somalia.d:
Somalia's documented case is about Turkey reaching into its schools. Turkey treats the Gülen movement, a religious network that ran schools in many countries, as a terrorist group and blames it for the 2016 coup attempt in Turkey. By June 2017 the movement's schools in Somalia had been taken over by Turkey's state Maarif Foundation after talks through Turkey's Foreign Ministry, as also happened in Guinea, Niger and Sudan. The handover is confirmed by Turkish government and Maarif statements.

Other organisations are recorded as present without a documented case here: the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist movement; the Order of Malta; and the security companies of Erik Prince, founder of the US firm Blackwater. Somalia's conditions scores are among the worst on the map: a high chance of powerful groups sitting inside the state and very weak checks.

Somalia sits in the patterns on Turkey's pursuit of the Gülen movement and churches and movements in the state.
Somalia.imp: A foreign government decided who would run schools that Somali children attended. The decision was driven from Ankara. With very weak checks, other outside forces could be present without being recorded. Watch what role foreign security firms and governments play in Somalia's security forces. Little else is documented yet, which reflects how hard it is to see inside the state.

South Africa.d: The main route in here runs through the state-owned companies and the tax service. Eskom, which supplies the country's electricity, and Transnet, which runs the ports and freight railways, buy on a scale that makes a bribe worth paying, and several foreign firms have now admitted paying one: a German software company, a Swiss-Swedish engineering group and two American consultancies, which between them have paid out hundreds of millions of dollars in US settlements.
