Two other large networks were designated in the same period, each with a legitimate business face.

The 1980s entry is different in kind: a group headed by the armed forces commander took money from a front for the Unification Church while taking over university, labour and peasant bodies.
Honduras.imp: When the head of state is in the trade there is no office above the problem to appeal to, and police protection that should be neutral is sold by the chief. Depositors in a bank liquidated because its owners were launderers lose access to their own money while payouts are arranged. A pardon granted by a foreign president can undo a sentence Hondurans had no say in, leaving the verdict on paper and the man at liberty, which is why the domestic arrest order matters.

Jamaica.d:
Two things are documented in Jamaica, twenty years apart, and both show a government caught between a foreign demand and a domestic interest. In the 1980s most of the state's foreign-currency accounts and its US commodity financing ran through BCCI, a bank later closed worldwide for fraud. One of its officers told a US Senate committee that it handled every penny of foreign currency going into or out of Jamaica, and the Senate report lists large loans to the Bank of Jamaica and to the state oil firm. That is the whole of what is established here: one foreign bank sitting at the chokepoint of a country's hard currency.

In 2010 the government spent nine months resisting a US request to extradite Christopher Coke, head of an armed organisation based in the Tivoli Gardens district, and retained a Washington law firm to lobby against it. The security operation that followed killed at least 69 people. Coke pleaded guilty in New York. A commission of enquiry found the operation's conduct unjustified, and the prime minister had already resigned over the affair before it reported.
Jamaica.imp: A single bank holding all of a country's foreign currency means its collapse becomes the country's problem and its records are the only account of where the money went. The extradition fight shows the other cost: a district leader who can deliver votes can buy a government's lawyers, and when the standoff finally breaks it is the people living in his district who are shot. The findings came after the prime minister had gone, which is the usual order here.

Mexico.d: Organised crime is the main outside force inside the Mexican state, and it works at every level rather than at the top alone. The method is a payroll: a police commander, a prosecutor, a judge, a prison director paid to look away or to act. Where a whole municipal force has been bought, the remedy is administrative — disarmed, disbanded or federalised — so most of it leaves no conviction behind. A sitting governor of Sinaloa and nine other state officials, among them the mayor of the capital and a serving senator, now face a New York indictment over a protection arrangement with one cartel faction; he denies it, resigned days later, and Mexico calls the evidence insufficient. Most of the record comes from US courts and US sanctions lists rather than Mexican ones, because Mexican cases against senior figures tend not to hold: federal police arrested ten mayors and other Michoacán officials in 2009, and within two years the courts had released all of them for want of evidence. Cartel money also sits inside ordinary business — tequila distilleries, gas stations, customs brokerages, a Puerto Vallarta resort whose call centres sell fake timeshare resales to its own customers. Older channels run alongside: foreign oil traders and construction firms paying officials of the state oil company for contracts, and a secret Catholic group, El Yunque, named in press accounts as placing members in party leadership and a federal cabinet — claims the party denies and no court has tested.
Mexico.imp: If the prosecutor, the judge and the police chief are on the same payroll, reporting a crime can be the most dangerous thing you do. Avocado and lime growers pay a fee per hectare and per shipment to people the state does not stop. Fuel from an ordinary station, pills from a licensed pharmacy and a timeshare contract can all belong to the same network. Watch whether cases against senior officials end in a Mexican verdict or only in a US filing.

Nicaragua.d: What is documented in Nicaragua is mostly outside states working on the institutions that deal with people directly. Russia's Interior Ministry runs a police training centre in the Las Colinas district of Managua, set up as an affiliate of the Russian ministry and attended at its opening by the president's son; it has trained Nicaraguan police and later officers from elsewhere in Central America and the Caribbean. The US Treasury sanctioned the centre in 2024, saying it teaches the Russian government's methods of suppressing civil society. The other direction is older and runs through money for politics. The National Endowment for Democracy, a foundation funded by the US government, put about $2 million into Nicaragua's civic opposition in the 1980s, roughly half of it to the newspaper run by Violeta Chamorro, who went on to win the 1990 election; Congress voted further money to boost the opposition shortly before that vote. The endowment says its grants are public and nonpartisan, and critics compared them to earlier covert operations in Chile. Banking left a mark too: a Luxembourg-held unit of Banco Ambrosiano, the Italian bank that collapsed in 1982, was licensed here and lent to both the Somoza government and the Sandinistas, until a presidential decree cancelled its licence in 1985.
Nicaragua.imp: Police training shapes how officers behave at a protest or a roadblock, so who does the training is not a technicality. Foreign money for newspapers and parties means some voices in an election are louder because a government abroad paid for them, and it hands whoever is in power a reason to call every critic foreign-funded. What to watch is which outside bodies are allowed to operate here and which get shut down.

Panama.d: Panama's position is what gets bought here: a banking system, a shipping corridor and a legal profession that can move money and goods with little trace. Offshore company formation is the clearest case. Mossack Fonseca, the firm at the centre of the Panama Papers, was tried at home and its founders acquitted in 2024, the judge citing insufficient and improperly gathered evidence. The firm that replaced it as the region's largest incorporator then turned up across the Pandora Papers, having built thousands of structures without verifying who owned them; it says it followed the law in force at the time and faces no charge. Goods move the same way through the Colón Free Zone, the largest free zone in the Americas, where cargo passes without entering Panamanian customs territory. Beneficial-ownership rules have been tightened and the volume has not fallen. The older record set the template. General Manuel Noriega held about $25 million in a bank account opened in the name of the national defence forces, and had the same bank pay off the mortgage of the man he chose as president. The current case is construction money: the Brazilian builder Odebrecht says tens of millions went to Panamanian officials, and the main laundering trial opened in 2026 with a former president taking part by video from asylum in Colombia.
Panama.imp: A system built to hide ownership hides it for everyone, so the bribe, the stolen contract and the ordinary tax dodge use the same lawyer and the same shell company. When the money goes, the road or the hospital it was meant to pay for is not built. An acquittal on procedural grounds leaves people no clearer about what actually happened. Watch whether the ownership rules now on paper change who gets registered in practice.

Paraguay.d: Paraguay sits on a cocaine corridor and at the corner of the Tri-Border Area with Brazil and Argentina, and what gets bought here is the part of the state that would otherwise stop the cargo. A laundering and cocaine investigation opened in 2022, A Ultranza Py, charged police officers, a serving prosecutor, court officials and a sitting member of the Chamber of Deputies, and seized hundreds of properties; several principals fled before arrest and one of the case's own prosecutors was later removed. Trade is the other channel. In the free-zone import-export business at Ciudad del Este, invoices and value move without matching cargo; Argentina froze one network's assets and the US designated its principals. In 2023 the US Treasury sanctioned a former president and the sitting vice-president for corruption, saying both had ties to members of Hizballah, the Lebanese armed movement and party, and that their representatives collected bribes at events it held in the country. The sanctions on the former president were lifted in 2025. The dictatorship left its own residue: in 1992 a lawyer and a judge found the secret police archive in a station outside Asunción, which proved Operation Condor — the coordinated hunt for exiles run by South America's military governments — had existed, and gave a later truth commission the names of 9,923 victims.
Paraguay.imp: When the prosecutor and the judge are part of the network, a seizure or an arrest is not the end of anything: the file stalls and the person charged leaves the country. Border trade nobody checks means honest importers compete with businesses whose cargo and paperwork do not match, and pay the same costs without the same margins. What to watch is whether the 2022 case reaches a verdict or quietly expires.

Peru.d: In Peru it is the courts that outside forces reach most often. Wiretaps set on a Callao trafficking group in 2018 picked up a separate network on the same lines — a supreme court judge, the president of the Callao superior court and members of the council that appoints and promotes judges, trading sentence reductions and posts. The judge fled to Spain, the court president was jailed, and the first conviction after a full trial came seven years later, with several implicated judges still sitting while under investigation. Construction money reaches the presidency: one former president is serving twenty years for taking about $35 million from the Brazilian builder Odebrecht in return for a highway contract, and another was convicted with his wife in 2025 of laundering tied to the same company. Both deny it. Religious and fraternal organisations place people openly rather than covertly. Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members seek holiness in ordinary work, has had members as production and defence minister, as a cardinal appointed a state mediator by Fujimori, and as mayor of Lima and now senator; membership is lawful and is not itself wrongdoing. The template was set by Vladimiro Montesinos, Fujimori's intelligence chief, who ran the service nominally responsible for counter-narcotics, was convicted of drug trafficking among dozens of counts, and videotaped himself paying the bribes — which is why so much of that record exists at all.
Peru.imp: If a judge's promotion depends on a favour, the outcome of your case may be settled before the hearing. A highway bought with a bribe gets built where the bribe wanted it, at the price the bribe allowed, and is paid for out of public money. Coca growers sell to traffickers partly because the state company licensed to buy the leaf pays less than traffickers do. Watch how long a case against a judge or a president takes to reach a verdict.

Trinidad and Tobago.d: No case of an outside force reaching into Trinidad and Tobago's own government is documented on this map, so this write-up is an estimate. The one case recorded here runs the other way, into an international body: Jack Warner sat in the cabinet as works minister and then national security minister while he was a vice-president of FIFA, football's world governing body, and a 2013 report by its regional confederation found he had committed fraud against it. US prosecutors indicted him in 2015 for wire fraud, racketeering and laundering, and Trinidad's High Court blocked his extradition in 2025. Likely but unshown here: energy-sector contracting and cocaine transit money.
Trinidad and Tobago.imp: An extradition blocked at home means a case with a US indictment behind it may never be heard anywhere, and the public never learns what a minister did while holding the national security portfolio. For an economy built on oil and gas contracting, the standing risk is who gets the licences and on what terms. What to watch is whether offices held abroad and offices held in cabinet are kept apart.

United States.d: More outside forces have a documented hand inside the United States than any other country on this map, and its own agencies and firms reach into other states. Foreign governments here work mostly through money and access rather than planted officers: lobbying registered late or not at all, donations routed through middlemen, paid trips and fees. China's effort is the widest — consulate-directed pressure on diaspora critics, an unregistered police outpost in Manhattan, aides inside state and city offices — with Russia, Iran, Turkey, Egypt, the Gulf states and both Koreas also present. Cases have reached senators, congressmen, a big-city mayor, ambassadors and party fundraisers of both parties, though several ended in acquittal or dismissal. Inside the country, the pattern is overlap, not espionage. People move between industries and the agencies that regulate them; model bills written by outside groups arrive at statehouses ready to vote, more than 10,000 traced in one review; banks, casinos and money transmitters take criminal deposits and settle; narcotics squads in several cities were convicted of running the drug trade they policed. Policy institutes supply staff to administrations of both parties, and a conservative legal society has been the acknowledged source for judicial nominations. The older layer is finance and fraternity: Morgan-led rescues of the Treasury, bankers drafting the Federal Reserve plan in private, lodges and the 1920s Klan choosing governors and a Supreme Court justice. That history also feeds a claim that a few banking families secretly own the Federal Reserve; its governors are appointed by the president and confirmed by the Senate.
United States.imp: Rules arrive already written by the people they will govern, so a utility bill or a pesticide decision reflects a company's draft rather than a hearing. Opioid shipments kept growing while the agency meant to stop them lost its strongest tool. People who left another country find its agents still watching them here. When a squad robs dealers, hundreds of convictions collapse. What to watch: who drafted the bill, and where a departing regulator goes to work.

Uruguay.d: Uruguay's documented record is thin, and most of it belongs to the military years of 1973 to 1985. Two arrivals in 1981 give the shape of it. Licio Gelli, head of the Italian masonic lodge Propaganda Due, fled to Montevideo with an Italian arrest warrant behind him; Uruguayan police seized his files at his villa, and most of the archive was never recovered. The same year the Unification Church, the religious movement founded by Sun Myung Moon, bought 49 percent of Banco de Credito, one of the country's oldest banks, and launched a daily paper that declared itself behind the military government. A parliamentary commission later found the bank had lent about $100 million to church-linked companies; it closed in 2002. Uruguayan and Italian courts have since convicted the dictatorship's own people: a former de facto president and a former foreign minister are both sentenced over disappearances carried out under Operation Condor, the arrangement through which South America's military governments handed prisoners to each other. What is live now runs the other direction. A tobacco company sued the country at a World Bank tribunal over its cigarette warning labels and lost in 2016, which is why Uruguay gets cited whenever a government wonders whether a health law is worth the legal risk.
Uruguay.imp: The bank case cost depositors and taxpayers: a bank lending heavily into its owner's own network failed, and the public system absorbed it. The Condor convictions came decades after the disappearances, so families waited most of their lives for a court to say what happened. The tobacco suit shows the quieter cost of being right. Defending a rule about cigarette packets took the government six years of international arbitration before it won, and smaller countries watch that bill.

Venezuela.d: Venezuela is the clearest case on this map of outside hands reaching all the way to the head of state, and of several reaching at once. For years the arrangement ran through the army and the police: US prosecutors say a network they call the Cartel de los Soles, after the suns on a general's epaulettes, runs through the officer corps itself, and they have charged a president, an interior minister and an intelligence chief, among more than a dozen officials, with moving cocaine. A few of those cases rest on guilty pleas; most have never been tested at trial, and analysts who accept that officials are involved in the trade dispute that a formal cartel exists. Alongside that sits one state's service inside another's. Documents show Cuba's defence ministry agreed in 2008 to rebuild Venezuela's military counterintelligence and train its officers in Havana, after which the service turned to watching Venezuela's own soldiers. Money has its own channels: an executive of a Brazilian construction firm told prosecutors the company put $35 million into a presidential campaign in return for priority on its projects, a claim the government rejects and no Venezuelan court has examined. Then the state itself became the target. The United States ran covert action inside the country, struck boats at sea, and in January 2026 seized Nicolas Maduro in Caracas and flew him to New York. Three days later it announced a deal to market Venezuelan oil into US-controlled accounts.
Venezuela.imp: When the national anti-drug office is run by someone prosecutors say was tipping off traffickers, there is nowhere to report a trafficker. When a military intelligence service is rebuilt to watch soldiers, it is not watching crime. Venezuelans have lived through default, a collapsed currency and mass emigration while public contracts went to firms that paid. What to watch now is who receives the new oil licences, and whether any of these cases is ever tried in a Venezuelan court.

Kosovo.d:
Kosovo's two documented cases are about what the war left behind and about Turkey. In December 2010 a Council of Europe rapporteur, the Swiss senator Dick Marty, reported that a Drenica Group of former Kosovo Liberation Army commanders, which he said was led by the then prime minister Hashim Thaçi, controlled criminal trades including heroin, and he described credible and converging indications of organ trafficking from captives after the 1999 war. The Parliamentary Assembly endorsed the report; Thaçi denied it. An EU task force that followed led to the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, where he has been on trial for war crimes since 2023. The organised-crime claims themselves have never been tested in court, and that has to be said plainly.

The second case is a foreign government reaching into Kosovo's own agencies. Turkey's government treats the movement of the preacher Fethullah Gülen as a terrorist organisation and has pursued its followers abroad since the 2016 coup attempt. In 2018 Kosovo police and intelligence seized five teachers and a doctor accused of Gülen links and flew them to Turkey on a private plane. The prime minister said he had not been told, and sacked the interior minister and the intelligence chief; a court later jailed the former intelligence chief for abuse of office.
Kosovo.imp: Claims about a wartime network that no court has tested leave people unable to know what their leaders did, which suits both the accused and the accusers. The 2018 deportations are concrete: six residents were taken out of the country without a hearing, by Kosovo's own police, for a foreign government. Watch whether extraditions go through the courts, and what the specialist chambers find.
